title: States dressing analysis in a transmon-transmon-bus system
authors: P. A. Gladilovich, R. A. Migdisov, A. V. Sabluk, P. S. Burtsev, N. N. Abramov, N. Y. Rudenko, V. I. Chichkov, N. A. Maleeva
abstract: The multi-qubit gates fidelity of superconducting quantum processors can be limited due to the dressing of computational states by noncomputational ones. Here, we experimentally and analytically investigate a transmon-transmon-bus system where the computational states dressing is tunable over a broad range. We estimate the dressing using three methods: a full three-element model, an effective mode approach, and an unperturbed mode approach. The obtained results highlight the importance of the accurate estimation and control of the computational states dressing in order to optimize gates on superconducting platform.
summary: The research investigates state dressing—the contamination of desired computational states by unwanted higher-energy modes—in a transmon-transmon-bus quantum processor. By comparing three estimation methods (full, effective, unperturbed), the authors demonstrate that accurate characterization of this dressing is vital for optimizing gate fidelity. The findings emphasize that simple approximations fail near critical operating points, necessitating full system analysis.
main_problem: The fidelity of multi-qubit gates in superconducting quantum processors is limited by the 'dressing' of computational states by unwanted noncomputational states.
main_result: Accurate estimation and control of this state dressing are crucial for optimizing gate operations, as different theoretical methods yield varying estimates depending on the operating regime.
method: The study compares three distinct analytical/numerical methods—full-system calculation, effective mode approach, and unperturbed mode approach—to quantify the participation weight (dressing) of noncomputational states.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a transmon-transmon-bus superconducting quantum processor comprising a qubit (Q), a coupler (C), and a resonator bus. The analysis uses the full Hamiltonian describing these coupled elements.
key_observables: Dressing weight ($D$), effective couplings ($g_{Q-U}^{	ext{eff}}$, $g_{Q-L}^{	ext{eff}}$), and mode frequencies ($f_U, f_L$).
important_parameters: The critical point ($f_c^U$) where spectral ordering inverts and effective couplings become equal is a key parameter.
main_assumptions: The unperturbed-mode method is shown to underestimate the true dressing near the critical detuning, highlighting the need for full system characterization at operating points.
figures_summary: Figures compare the three methods for estimating $D$ across varying frequencies ($f_U$), showing how the calculated dressing changes dramatically around a critical frequency region. Other figures map out effective couplings vs. mode frequencies.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of state dressing, details the physical transmon-bus model, and then systematically compares the results from three different theoretical estimation techniques (full, effective, unperturbed) across varying system parameters to determine the most reliable characterization method for gate optimization.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete experimental and analytical guidance on mitigating decoherence sources in superconducting qubits by quantifying how non-computational states pollute the computational subspace, which is central to scaling quantum processors.
